title: As an offering
hook: whatever you do, eat, give, do it as an offering (Bhagavad Gita 9.27)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gita's line on your own duty: better your own, done imperfectly, than another's done well. Your line was my own work. Did you catch yourself comparing? Day eight hundred ninety-three.

A leaf. A flower. A piece of fruit. A little water. In the ninth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna names these small things and says that when they're offered with devotion, he accepts them. The verse asks only that it be given with devotion. Nothing on the list is costly. And then, a verse later, Krishna widens it past anything that could fit on a plate. Not only leaves and flowers. Everything. Today's word is what happens when the whole working day becomes the plate.
screen: `A LEAF, A FLOWER, FRUIT, WATER.` → `OFFERED WITH DEVOTION.` → `THEN, EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in paraphrase: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in worship, whatever you give away, whatever discipline you practice, do it as an offering to me. First, notice the list. It starts with doing, and eating comes second. Not prayer, not ritual. The ordinary verbs of a day come first. The Sanskrit word for this kind of offering is arpana, something handed over, given up to God. Second, what changes. The work itself might not change at all. The same report, the same pot of rice, the same shift. What changes is who it's for. In the Gita, a deed done as an offering isn't done mainly for praise, or pay, or even for the result. The next verse says that by doing this a person is freed from the bonds that actions bring, good or bad. Third, who is speaking. In the Gita, Krishna speaks as God. Hindus who worship Krishna hear the verse as a direct invitation to give him everything. Readers from other Hindu schools understand the 'me' in their own ways, and the Gita has been read by commentators from different directions. Fourth, where the verse lands. A nurse taking a pulse. A student writing an essay at midnight. Someone folding laundry for a family that won't say thanks. In the Gita's picture, any of these can be laid down like a flower. Not because the task is grand, but because of how it's handed over. Back to the opening: a leaf is enough. So is one task, done and given away.
screen: `WHATEVER YOU DO, EAT, GIVE.` · `THE SAME TASK, A NEW ADDRESS.` · `KRISHNA SPEAKS AS GOD.` · `A TASK LAID DOWN LIKE A FLOWER.` · then, large: `DO IT AS AN OFFERING.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath find its own pace. Pick one task waiting for you today. Something ordinary: a meal, a message, a repair, a page of work. Picture yourself doing it slowly and well. Now picture handing it over when it's done, the way you'd set a flower down. To God, if that's your way, or to the people it serves, or simply to the day. Breathe in, holding it. Breathe out, letting it go. If you pray, you can offer it in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
As an offering. From the Bhagavad Gita: whatever you do, eat or give, do it as an offering. The Sanskrit is arpana. Today's word.
Your line: as an offering. Today, offer one task. Before you start it, decide who it's for, and when it's done, let it go. Day eight hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Hindus offer food, flowers, water or a lamp to God at home shrines and temples, and some dedicate their daily work in the spirit of Gita 9.27.

original.note: Sanskrit, from the Hindu tradition: an offering, something handed over to God (Gita 9.27).

trapdoor: what you thought: an offering is something you bring to a temple.
what it means: in the Gita, any act, eating, giving, working, can be handed over to God as an offering.
what a scholar hears: the list puts doing and eating first, and the next verse says such acts free a person from the bonds of their results.

notes: Gita 9.26–9.28 paraphrased; confirm the order of the list in 9.27 (do, eat, offer, give, austerity) and the 9.28 paraphrase.
Original: अर्पण (arpana); the verse uses mad-arpanam. Confirm gloss and transliteration.
'Readers from other Hindu schools understand the me in their own ways' is deliberately general; a Hindu Keeper may name schools.
howItsDone describes home and temple offerings in general terms.
